questions.q: What are the four required deliverables for the capstone project?
options: A from-scratch derivation, a small-scale simulation you run yourself, at least one independently verified numeric claim, and an honest benchmarking section
A literature review, a slide deck, a peer review, and a final exam
A derivation, a video recording, a group presentation, and a bibliography
A simulation only, with no derivation or benchmarking required
questions.explain: The brief specifies exactly four deliverables: derivation, simulation, verified numeric claim, and honest benchmarking section, modeled on how this course built every chapter.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say plain Node.js matrix arithmetic is a legitimate approach for the capstone's simulation deliverable, rather than a workaround?
options: Because this exact approach was used throughout the course itself to compute the Grover tables, the QFT matrix, the phase-estimation probabilities, and the Shor's-algorithm sequences
Because Python is the only other option and it is not installed
Because matrix arithmetic is required by the course platform's technical specifications
Because Qiskit and other quantum frameworks cannot run small simulations
questions.explain: The course modeled exactly this approach in every chapter — implementing the actual oracle/diffusion matrices, the QFT matrix, and the inverse-QFT probability formula directly, rather than relying on a specialized framework.

questions.q: What does the grading rubric's 'Verification rigor' criterion check for?
options: Whether the derivation is longer than two pages
Whether the claimed numeric result was actually computed and shown, rather than merely asserted
Whether the simulation uses a specific programming language
Whether the write-up uses advanced vocabulary
questions.explain: Verification rigor specifically checks that a stated number was the result of an actual computation shown in the work, not a plausible-looking guess — consistent with the course's verification discipline throughout.

questions.q: According to the capstone lesson's closing summary, what is the actual skill this course has been teaching, beyond the six named algorithms?
options: Proving that quantum computers are always faster than classical computers
Memorizing the exact probability values from every chapter's examples
Computing the real number before stating it, and saying precisely what is and isn't true about a result once you have it
Writing quantum circuits exclusively in Qiskit
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states the throughline: verify before claiming, and be precise about what is and isn't established — a skill that transfers beyond the six specific algorithms covered.

questions.q: Why must the capstone's benchmarking section use Lesson 31's checklist and Lesson 33's template rather than a free-form comparison?
options: Because free-form writing is not permitted anywhere in the course
Because the template is required by the course platform's software

Because the structured template forces naming a real classical baseline, stating the precise metric, and ending with a hedged verdict, preventing the kind of overstated claim the course has repeatedly warned against
Because only Lesson 31 and Lesson 33 contain any numeric data
questions.explain: The structured approach is what prevents an unsupported or oversold conclusion — exactly the discipline modeled in Lessons 31 and 33 and applied throughout the rest of the course.
